title: Security Misconfiguration
brief: **Ticket:** the app ships without security headers. Identify the header that stops MIME sniffing.
theory:
## What it is
Security Misconfiguration (OWASP A05) is being insecure by default: missing
security headers, verbose error pages, default credentials, unnecessary features
left on, or storage left open to the world.

## How it works
A response with no `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, or
`X-Frame-Options` leaves the app open to clickjacking, MIME sniffing, and weaker
XSS defence. Stack traces shown to users leak internal paths and versions.
Default admin passwords and open cloud buckets need no "exploit" at all.

## In the real world
Thousands of publicly readable **Amazon S3 buckets** have leaked customer data
simply because the default/chosen configuration was "public". Misconfiguration is
consistently one of the most common findings in real assessments because it is
everywhere and easy to miss.

## How to prevent it
Harden by default: send security headers, disable debug/verbose errors in
production, change defaults, remove unused features, and review cloud resource
permissions. Bake these checks into CI so they cannot regress.
worked_example:
```
$ curl -s -D - https://good.example/ -o /dev/null | grep -i content-security
content-security-policy: default-src 'self'
```

knowledge_check.q: Error pages shown to users should be ___
Which header limits what scripts can load/run?

investigation.intro: Compare the response headers of the insecure app versus the hardened one.
steps:
**Start the lab app** (leave it running; open a *second* terminal tab for the attack):
```bash
cd /workspaces/examto/appsec-lab
python3 -m venv .venv 2>/dev/null; . .venv/bin/activate; pip install -q -r requirements.txt
python3 run_server.py
```

In a second terminal, look at the insecure response headers - note there is no CSP and no nosniff:
```bash
curl -s -D - "http://127.0.0.1:5000/health" -o /dev/null
```

**Apply the fix and re-test.** Stop the server (Ctrl+C) and restart it in secure mode, then run the SAME attack again:
```bash
LAB_SECURE=1 python3 run_server.py
```

Re-check the headers in secure mode and confirm the protections are now present:
```bash
curl -s -D - "http://127.0.0.1:5000/health" -o /dev/null | grep -iE "content-security|x-content-type|x-frame|referrer"
```
The capture asks you to name a header that was missing before.
hints: Use curl -D - to dump response headers.
Secure mode adds the headers the insecure mode lacked.

capture.task: **Name the control.** Which response header (its name) carries the value `nosniff`?
